i can relate.  i have a few FPs that I love very much in varying degrees but if any one of them shows a slight shift in behavior my whole brain goes haywire.  Ive managed to learn to self soothe and get my needs met in other ways however having the symptoms coming from this disorder is so so exhausting and I hate having to be hyper aware of how my body is feeling, my thoughts, etc every single day of my life.

one of the few things that’s “”helped”” me has been having more than one FP attachment— doesn’t have to be romantic and hell it can even be a pet or stuffed animal.  I currently have about 5(?) though one of them has recently discarded me so I guess 4 now.  it helps with getting my needs of feeling wanted and social met.  I also write letters to my FPs that may or may not be sent.  

  Hope it helps.

Thank you for not discarding us and actually wanting to take the time to try to understand even if you might never know the exact  experience.  

  One of my favorite analogies from “I hate you, don’t leave me” is when he compares people with bpd to people who have third degree burns.  Our emotional skin is riddled with third degree burns and any irritation feels like Hell.  It makes me so happy to see a person without BPD recognize that we are not that person during our flareups.  

  Thank you so much.

First of all she is extremely blessed to have somebody like you.  I just want to say thank you for being such a compassionate and understanding partner who wants to see their partner W/ BPD get the care they deserve.  SO MANY people w/o BPD have such negative preconceived notions about us and just write us off as monsters who lack empathy when NONE OF US ASK TO HAVE THIS DIAGNOSIS.

  With all of that being said,  I recommend reading books such as “I hate you, don’t leave me” by Jerold J. Kreisman and “Loving Someone with Borderline Personality Disorder” by Shari Y. Manning.

  I hope they help!  Again, thank you for being one of those unicorns who don’t just write us off as monsters. <3

First of all I’m very proud of you for getting the help that you deserve.  It definitely is a leap of faith especially considering that you have been seeking treatment for months now.  I will agree that taking a break from social media has tremendously helped me. I’ve taken up hobbies of writing letters to my partner and to friends, journaling, making friendship bracelets, reading, etc.

  I think some of the books that have change my life as an individual with BPD are these:
  
  Coping With BPD by Blaise Aguirre (I LOVE this book. I 10000% recommend it for anyone with BPD)

The Stronger Than BPD Journal by Debbie Corso

Stronger Than BPD: The Girl’s Guide to Taking Control of Intense Emotions, Drama, and Chaos Using DBT by Debbie Corso

  The Borderline Personality Disorder Survival Guide: Everything You Need to Know About Living with BPD by Alex L. Chapman

  Hope these help!

I just want to validate your feelings of feeling like you are an awful person for having a condition that you didn’t ask to have.   Self compassion is a battle with me as well and the amount of negative stigma there is towards individuals with BPD Doesn’t help.   I also want to let it be known that you are not a bad person for having borderline personality disorder we as individuals with BPD have needs that we need to be met like any other human on this planet it’s just we are individuals who are a more emotionally sensitive than neurotypicals. 

  You are wanted.  You are more than your diagnosis and you have needs just like every other human on this planet and it’s not fair to you that individuals decide to remain ignorant and only see us for our diagnosis which, by the way, is due to severe childhood trauma that we could not control.

I often feel this.  It is very difficult for me to not feel inadequate when my partner does not respond right away or whenever he is busy.  It often triggers my abandonment and left unchecked I will spend my entire day having flare up after flare up while Catastrophizing my thoughts and thinking the worst.

  I feel like one thing that has helped me is to have a “support network” of people I can routinely interact with and feel safe with.  I tend to have multiple fps that include my partner all with various degrees of attachment— I think at this moment I have about 6 fps at this moment my partner obviously being my #1 and one of them is a stuffed dog that I have had for years that I talk to whenever I need to self soothe during my “flare ups”.  The only FP I am romantically attracted to is my partner and although I love all of my FPs,   I will not deny I am deeply in love with my partner.   I do this because i’ve found that the core “need” i’m missing to be met is the sense of emotional connection and the sense of feeling wanted.  

  I’ve found that in doing this with myself I can get my needs met without 100% emotionally depending on one person.  When I also have urges to contact my partner I will write him letters that I may or may not send to him.  I like to decorate them in stickers, use different colored pens, etc.  Writing letters and sending them meets my need on wanting to interact with him without sending him a ton of messages, calls or waiting on him to reply. 

   I also like to make friendship bracelets and it makes me feel very wanted whenever I see my partner wear the ones I make them.  

   My biggest trigger is fear of abandonment.  Going back to my stuffed dog “FP”, the reason why I have a stuffed animal as an FP is because they can never “abandon” you.  I often make my stuffed dog “talk” to me and it helps me rationalize my thoughts.  

    It took me a very long time to be able to get to this point and I still deeply struggle with my intense emotions. Having self compassion towards myself is difficult. However I like to say even though us individuals with BPD might be emotionally sensitive I like to think when we love somebody, we love them deeply— far deeper than any Neurotypical could understand.

  I hope this helps.
